nodes.name: RES drying and crushing
nodes.procedure: The collected RES sample was firstly dried at 60 °C for 24 h to achieve constant weight and crushed into small particles less than 0.15 mm.
nodes.source_text: The collected RES sample was firstly dried at 60 °C for 24 h to achieve constant weight and crushed into small particles less than 0.15 mm.

nodes.name: CES calcination (500°C)
nodes.procedure: The [dried and crushed] sample was calcined in a tubular furnace (KSY-6-16 A, Tianjin Zhonghuan Co., Ltd., China) for 2 h at 500 °C under nitrogen atmosphere while the pyrolysis heating rate was set at 10 °C/min. RES after calcination at 500 °C was designated as CES.

nodes.name: SCES preparation and calcination
nodes.procedure: The simulated calcination electroplating sludge (SCES) was prepared in ultrapure water using the following reagents: FeSO₄·7H₂O, CaO, CrCl₃·6H₂O, Cu(NO₃)₂·3H₂O, NiSO₄·6H₂O, KH₂PO₄, NaOH and citric acid (citric acid was chosen as the representative organic matter in the electroplating sludge). The molar ratios of Fe, Ca, Cr, Cu, Ni and P were based on their detection concentrations in the real electroplating sludge (Table 2). The prepared sludge was dried at 60 °C for 24 h to a constant weight and crushed into 0.15 mm particles. Finally, the dried simulation electroplating sludge was calcined at 500 °C under nitrogen atmosphere.

nodes.description: Ni(II)-citrate removal from electroplating wastewater in CES/H2O2 system
nodes.source_text: With the addition of 50 mmol/L H2O2 and 1.5 g/L CES, 87% of the total nickel could be removed within 50 min when the total nickel concentration in the Ni(II)-citrate containing electroplating wastewater was 283 mg/L

nodes.description: CES dosage effect on Ni(II)-citrate removal
nodes.source_text: The removal efficiency of nickel increased from 62% to 96% when the dosage of CES increased from 1.0 to 2.5 g/L

nodes.description: H2O2 dosage effect on Ni(II)-citrate removal
nodes.source_text: the nickel removal efficiencies increased from 55% to 93% within 50 min when the H2O2 dosage varied from 25 to 100 mmol/L

nodes.description: pH effect on Ni(II)-citrate removal (pH range 2.82-7.63)
nodes.source_text: The best removal was achieved at pH 7.63. In contrast, the removal of total nickel was very low at the initial pH 2.82 or 4.79

nodes.description: Comparison of different systems for Ni(II)-citrate removal
nodes.source_text: 87% total nickel could be removed at 50 min in the CES/H2O2 system... only 32% of total nickel was removed within 50 min... Neither CES nor RES alone could effectively remove Ni(II)-citrate

nodes.characterization_summary: Fresh CES elemental composition: Fe 18.24 wt%, Ca 19.37 wt%, Cr 4.29 wt%, Cu 7.69 wt%, Ni 3.92 wt%, P 2.99 wt%.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Table 2 Elemental compositions of the RES, pristine and spent CES by XRF analysis.

nodes.characterization_summary: CES surface area 55.3 m²/g, pore volume 0.315 cm³/g, most pores <2 nm (micropores).
nodes.evidence_snippet: The surface area and pore volume of the CES were measured to be 55.3 m²/g and 0.315 cm³/g, respectively. The pore size distribution of CES is shown in Fig. S1a, and the sizes of most pores were less than 2 nm (micropores).

nodes.characterization_summary: CES zeta potential negative in pH range 4.91-9.32, favorable for adsorption of positively charged heavy metals.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The zeta potentials of CES (Fig. S1b) show that the CES surfaces were negative in the pH range of 4.91-9.32, favorable for the adsorption of positively charged heavy metals in the wastewater via electrostatic attraction.

nodes.characterization_summary: CES surfaces covered with spherical particles of 20-50 nm diameter.
nodes.evidence_snippet: According to the SEM images (Fig. S2), ... the CES surfaces were covered with spherical particles with diameters of 20-50 nm

nodes.characterization_summary: CES shows peaks from copper ferrite (CuFe₂O₄), nickel ferrite (NiFe₂O₄), and magnetite (Fe₃O₄).
nodes.evidence_snippet: As calcination temperature increased, the obvious peaks originated from copper ferrite (CuFe₂O₄), nickel ferrite (NiFe₂O₄) and magnetite (Fe₃O₄) could be observed on the CES

nodes.characterization_summary: CES shows weakened OH stretch at 3443 cm⁻¹, H₂O bend at 1644 cm⁻¹, C=O stretch at 1488-1424 cm⁻¹, PO₄³⁻ at 1060 cm⁻¹, and enhanced metal oxide bands at 558-611 cm⁻¹.
nodes.evidence_snippet: FTIR measurement was carried out to investigate the functional groups on the surface of RES and CES (Fig. 1b).

nodes.characterization_summary: Pristine CES shows surface elements Fe, Ca, Cu, Cr; after reaction Ni 2p peaks appear at 854-890 eV, Cu 2p3/2 shifts 932.6→932.2 eV, Fe 2p3/2 shifts 711.6→711.2 eV indicating Cu(II)→Cu(I) and Fe(III)→Fe(II) reduction.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The XPS spectra of the pristine CES in Fig. S6a revealed that the major metal elements on the surface of CES were Fe, Ca, Cu and Cr, consistent with the result of XRF analysis. After the decomplexation and adsorption processes, the strong peaks of Ni 2p clearly appeared at 890-854 eV

nodes.characterization_summary: Organic content (C,H,O,N) in CES significantly decreased after pyrolysis.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The organic elemental compositions of the RES and CES were summarized in Table S2. During the pyrolysis process, the contents of C, H, O and N decreased significantly
